about: The words of the chain tiel_1020 (Data/encounters/chain_tiel_1020_793.json; Design/content/chains/tiel_1020.md): the sworn merchants of Tiel after Vlaardingen, 1018 to 1030, as the monk Alpert complained of them, and a seat among them. Every title, intention, line and label key of its fourteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', with _success and _failure where there is a chance, named in each option's note); two news items; a picture line for every card (art.<card id>) and for every ending (art.chain_tiel_1020.ending.<name>). Nothing is quoted from a modern book; Alpert's sense is given in our own words. A draft for the user to overwrite. Written 6 Oct 2026.

entries.text: The closed fist

On the bank an Englishman asks a Tiel merchant for the price of twelve sacks of wool. The Tiel man holds up a closed fist and swears he owes nothing. Six men of Tiel step up and swear with him. Nobody seems surprised but the Englishman.
Twelve sacks, shorn at midsummer, weighed on his own beam. He said: after the herring. The herring has come and gone and so, it seems, has my wool.
I swear by God and Saint Walburg that I owe this man nothing. There. It is sworn, and these six swear I swear true. That is how a thing is ended where I come from.
You. You were lying next to him when they went aboard. You have eyes. Did I dream twelve sacks?
Do not look for a court. We took our last complaint to the emperor himself, and what came of it lies in the ditches at Flardinga. Since then we settle things at home.
I know this one. He put pennies in our purse once, when it was for the complaint. Let him say what he likes. He paid for the right.
Say what you saw: twelve sacks went over his gunwale
Ask the Tiel man what a seat on that bench costs
Say nothing, and watch how it is done

You say it: twelve. One voice against seven. The oath stands, because there is nobody on this bank to make it fall. The Englishman grips your arm and tells you what he can give: wine is a third dearer in London than it was at Lammas.

The Tiel man laughs and opens his fist. It is empty. More than this, he says, and less than you fear. Come down to Tiel in three weeks, early, and ask for Sibrand. The Englishman spits and goes to his boat.
You watch. Seven oaths, one closed hand, and a debt is gone like frost off a thwart. A boy tells you they are Tiel men and it is always so. Come and see them at home, he says. They start early.

At Tiel a man who owes swears that he does not, and his fellows swear with him, and there the matter ends. A stranger will not win a case against one of them. They say the emperor wrote that they might. Nobody has seen the writing.
The morning cask

Sibrand takes you down the Waal to Tiel. The sun is not yet over the dyke. The bench by the stone toll house is already full, and the cask already open, and somebody is already shouting the end of a story.
We asked the emperor for help against the count. He sent three bishops' men and a duke into a marsh. Now we ask each other. It is cheaper, and nobody drowns.
The rule of the bench: the man who tells the foulest story loudest drinks free till noon. A priest once won. We do not say which priest.
There was a monk here last month for Saint Walburg's wonders. He looked at my cask the way you look at a leak. He wrote something down. I charged him double.
A seat. Two of us to swear you are what you say. A pound of pennies in the chest, counted on the cloak. And one year in which no brother has cause against you. That is all. It is not little.
You spoke against Wigbold on the bank. Good. Now I know you can count, and that you say the number aloud. We will see which side of the bench that is useful on.
This is the one who saw seven men swear and asked what it cost to be the eighth. I like him. He will go far or be hanged, and either way not at my cost.
Tell the one about what stands up in a bed and makes a wife weep
Pay for the next cask
Drink what is poured and listen

You tell it slowly: it stands tall in a bed, it is hairy below, a churl's daughter grips it, and her eye is wet. The bench roars before you say onion. An Englishman at the end scratches it on bark for you, as his own people have it in a book.
You say onion too soon. There is a silence, then Wigbold laughs at you and not at the story, which on this bench is worth nearly as much. Your cup is filled all the same.

Thirty pennies on the board and the ale-wife knocks the bung from a new cask. Nobody thanks you. Three men move up to make room, which is the thanks. Sibrand says their man in London should know your face before Easter.

You drink and listen until noon. You learn who owes whom, who is lying up for the winter, and that the bench keeps a man in London who is short of something. Sibrand says: go and see him. A seat starts with an errand.
The emperor's men
Below the bridge a Tiel man has a store of his own and a tally of what the bench owes the king's reeve before Easter. He is counting gloves, and coming out one pair short every time.
Here we are the emperor's men, and the law of this town says the emperor's men who come in their own ships have as good a law as a Londoner. I have heard it read. I had it read twice.

For that, at Christmas and again at Easter: two grey cloths and a brown one, ten pounds of pepper, five pairs of gloves, two kegs of vinegar. The gloves are for the reeve's men. They have very many hands.
Cloth I have. Vinegar makes itself. Pepper I have not. The Cologne boats are late and the reeve does not take a promise in place of a pound.
What did the count take from you at the mouth? No, do not tell me. Every keel from home tells me, and each time it is a little more, and each time I am told it is the last.
The king here is a Dane now. The reeve is the same reeve. The toll is the same toll. I have stopped asking who is king. I ask who is reeve.
Take the order: ten pounds of pepper for the reeve's due
Lend him 100 d against eight bolts of English cloth
Hear how the emperor's men stand in London, and promise nothing

He cuts a stick for ten pounds of pepper at six tenths over the price, to be here before the reeve asks twice. And he says, not looking up from the gloves: when Sibrand asks who will swear for you, he may say my name.

A hundred pennies cross the board. Eight bolts of good English cloth come back as a pledge he does not expect to redeem. He says he will swear for you at Tiel. A man who lends to the bench at need is already half on it.

He talks while he counts. Pepper will be dear here until the Rhine boats come. He gives you a leaf an English schoolmaster wrote, a merchant answering for his trade. It is the only kind word about us, he says, that I ever saw written down.
The count's man at the mouth
At the river mouth, under the count's fort, his man came aboard as he comes aboard every keel. This time he knew your name, and your cargo, and on which bench you had been drinking.
The count takes a toll here. The emperor said he might not, and sent an army to say it louder. You sailed in over that army. So: the toll.
I was on the dyke that day. They came ashore among the ditches in mail. Somebody shouted that the duke had fallen. After that we hardly had to do anything.

My lord is no robber. He sells cheese and wants English cloth, like anyone. Carry his cheese, pass here free, and tell me now and then what the Tiel bench means to do next. They are always meaning something.
You have paid here before without a face on you. I marked it. A man who pays without a sermon is a man the count can talk to.
Take the count's tally: his cheese to London, no toll at the mouth, and a word now and then
Tell him you carry cargo, not words, and pay as every keel pays
Refuse, and tell Sibrand that the count is buying ears

He counts out a hundred and twenty pennies and has twenty wheels of cheese swung into your hold. The tally he gives you is short and has three notches. Show it at the mouth, he says. Do not show it at Tiel.
He shrugs and takes the toll, no more than from anyone. Cargo, then, he says. It is a pity. Cargo pays once. He goes over the side to the next keel.

You pay, and at Tiel you tell Sibrand. He is not angry. He is pleased, the way a man is pleased to find the hole in his net. So the count wants to know what we mean to do, he says. Then we mean something.
A monk with a wax tablet

A monk waits by your boat with a tablet and a stylus. He has heard that you drink at Tiel. He asks his questions like a man who has already written the answers and wants only to be sure of the spelling.
I am Alpert. I am writing down what has happened in these parts in my own time, for a bishop on the Rhine who likes to know. Most of it is counts killing each other. Tiel is a rest from that.
Is it true that if a man can close his hand over a thing, he may swear with the other hand that he never had it? I was told so. I should like to hear it from someone sober.
They say the emperor gave them a charter to judge as they please. I have asked to see it. Each of them says another one keeps it. I have run out of Tiel men to ask.
I do not hate them. I wrote down their saint's wonders, and there are many. Saint Walburg is very patient at Tiel. She has to be.
Tell him all of it: the fist, the oath, the morning cask
Tell him the other half too: the chest buries a drowned brother and feeds his widow
Say a guest does not carry the bench out through the door

You tell him. His stylus does not stop. When you are done he reads it back in Latin and then in plain speech: hard men, used to no discipline, judging not by law but by their will. He has left your name out. He thinks that is a kindness.

You tell him the fist, and then the rest: the chest that buries a drowned man and keeps his widow in bread. He writes the first part quickly and the second part slowly. That will not fit my chapter, he says. But I will remember it.

He closes the tablet without anger. A guest's answer, he says, and a good one. But the ale-wife talks, and the Englishmen talk, and the page will be filled. He blesses your boat, which costs him nothing.
Seven hands
On the bank at Tiel a Cologne man says Wigbold had fifteen casks of him at Martinmas and has paid for six. You were there when they were rolled ashore. There were fifteen. Sibrand is looking at you.
Fifteen casks of the white, from above Andernach. My mark is burnt in every head. Nine of them I have not seen a penny for, and I have come down the river three times to say so.
Six I had and six I paid. If there were more casks on the bank that day they were another man's, or the river's. I will swear it now and save us all the afternoon.
Wigbold will swear, and six with him. I have five. You have drunk our ale since harvest. A man who wants a seat can show it today with one hand.
Seven hands. I know how it goes here. I ask only this: let one of the seven be a man who can count to fifteen.
You counted wool sacks aloud once, for an Englishman. I have not forgotten. Today I should like you to have forgotten how.
You told us the count was buying ears. That was a brother's act before you were a brother. I say so in front of them all. Now do the other thing a brother does.
Lay your hand with theirs and swear he owes nothing
Keep your hand down, and say the chest should pay him and take it back from Wigbold
Say you stood too far off to count, and keep your hand in your belt

Seven hands, and one of them yours. The Cologne man looks at you a long moment and goes to his boat without a word. That evening Wigbold counts a hundred and fifty pennies into your cap. It is the price of about four casks.

You say it plainly: pay him from the chest, and let Wigbold owe his brothers, who know where he sleeps. There is a long quiet. Then Sibrand laughs. We judge by our own will, he says. Today our will is to pay. Wigbold does not laugh.

You say it plainly, and nobody hears it. A sixth hand is found. The oath is sworn without you. The Cologne man nods to you as he leaves. Sibrand says nothing at all, and pours your cup a finger short.

You say you could not see for the sun. Sibrand finds another hand; there is always a hand. The oath is sworn. Nobody on the bank believes you about the sun, and both sides think a little less of you for it.
What Cologne remembers
Wezelo's cellar is under the old wall, cool and full. He knows your boat before she touches the strand, and he comes down to the water himself, wiping his hands.
The seventh hand. I have a good memory for hands. Buy what you like here; my silver does not know you. But nobody in this street will let a cask go to you on trust. I have seen to it.
I was paid. Nine casks, from their own chest, by their own will, because a man with a small boat said so. I told it in every cellar on this strand. Nobody believed me until I showed the pennies.
You kept your hand down. It did me no good and I do not forget it. A man who will not swear false is rare enough down there to be worth a cup. Sit.
We need them and they know it. Every cask for England goes past their toll house. So we sell to them, and we count twice, and once a year one of us is robbed with seven oaths.
There is one court a Tiel man cannot swear his way out of with his friends. Their church is the bishop of Traiectum's. A false oath is the bishop's business. I have had my claim written out.
Take his order: twelve casks down the river on your own name
Pay him for the nine casks out of your own chest, and say why
Offer to carry his claim to the bishop's court at Traiectum
Buy your wine like any stranger and say nothing of Tiel

He gives you eighty pennies of earnest and an order for twelve casks at half over the price, on your name and no other. I will sell to Tiel through you, he says. Then at least I know which hand to watch.

You count Wigbold's hundred and fifty onto his board and say what they were paid for. He does not touch them for a while. Then he sweeps them up, and has two casks rolled to your boat. You swore false and paid true, he says. I have known bishops do worse.
He gives you a folded sheet, sealed with a wine merchant's ring, and twenty pennies for the carrying. Give it to the bishop's clerk, he says, not to a Tiel man, and not to the river.
You buy and he sells. He says only that the potters' boats came down from Pingsdorf yesterday, all at once, and the grey ware is going for four fifths of its price until they are gone.
The common chest
The boats are drawn up at Tiel for the winter and the chest is carried out. Three men have its three keys. The year's gain is counted on a cloak, and Sibrand asks the bench what it should buy.
Every brother puts in. In spring it goes out again on the keels, to England, to Cologne. In winter it comes home fatter. What a man put in he takes out, and his part of the fat. The rest we drink.
A newcomer's pound goes on the cloak today, where all can see it counted. If you have not got it, sit down anyway. The cask does not ask.
I say what I say every year. Martinmas, Christmas, Easter, Pentecost: four feasts, and we get drunk at each one properly, as if it were laid on us. It is why God sent the gain.
The monks ask for our charter. The bishop will ask next. We have always said the emperor gave us one. My father said it. I have never held it in my hand, and I keep the chest.
This one put his hand with mine against the Cologne man. I ask no more of a brother. Let him count his pound and I will pour for him myself.
This one made the chest pay a stranger. It cost us nine casks, and the Cologne boats came down a week early this autumn. I have reckoned it. We are ahead.
There is a monk at Traiectum who knows what our cask looks like at sunrise. Somebody told him. I do not ask who. I say only that the bench has long ears, as well as a loud mouth.
Put in your pound, and let it be drunk as it always was
Put in your pound, and say: buy the writing you say you have
Put in your pound, and say: offer the count a fixed sum each Martinmas and be done
Keep your pound this winter and drink as a guest

Two hundred and forty pennies, counted on the cloak, twelve at a time. The lid comes down on them. Then the cask is opened, and nobody at Tiel does any work that could be called work until the third day.

You say it: the emperor is alive, the chancery sells calfskin, buy the thing you swear by. Wigbold shouts that it is a waste of good ale. Sibrand lets him finish. Then he says: after Easter, when the emperor is on the hill. And you will come, since it was your tongue.

You say it, and the bench laughs you down. Buy what we have had since the old emperor? Your pound stays on the cloak all the same. Sibrand does not laugh. He looks at the chest for a while, and then at the door of the church.

A sum to Dirk? There is a growl along the bench. Three years ago they would have thrown you in the Waal. Now nobody stands up. Sibrand says: the bench does not send to the count. If a man knew the count's steward, the bench would not ask where he had been.

You keep your pound, and you drink, and nobody counts your cups. A guest is a guest. Sibrand says the cloak will be spread again whenever you are ready, and that a bishop's clerk has been asking for the names of those who trade here.
What is to be written
The emperor is on the hill at Noviomagus. In the clerks' room a chaplain rules a sheet of calfskin and asks Sibrand what, exactly, the emperor is to have granted. Sibrand looks at you.
A charter says a thing, and afterwards it says that thing for ever. So. What do the merchants of Tiel want the emperor to have always meant?
All of it. That we judge whoever trades on our bank. That a brother's oath ends a debt. Write that, and no monk will ever ask me another question.
The bishop of Traiectum is in the hall today. If I write that an oath ends a debt, he will ask to read it before the seal. He reads quickly. I should not count on that sentence.

The merchants of Magdeburg have a writing from the emperor's father's time: free of toll everywhere, save four places. Yours is one of the four. Emperors remember Tiel. Ask for what an emperor can sign without frowning.
You follow the Latin. Then stand here by my elbow and follow it. Most men who buy a charter find out what it says from the next man who sues them.
Ask for what is true: Tiel men judge trade among themselves, and answer strangers before the king's man
Ask for all the bench claims: its own judgement over anyone who trades at Tiel, and the oath that clears a debt
Ask for what is true, and read the draft yourself before the seal goes on
Tell Sibrand the price is too high, and carry the chest home

The chaplain writes: that the merchants of Tiel may settle among themselves what belongs to their trade; that a stranger's claim goes before the king's man; that they are in the emperor's peace. The bishop reads it and hands it back. On the third day it comes down the hill with a seal.

The gifts go up the hill. Word comes down: the emperor rides for Saxony tomorrow and the matter can wait for his return. Forty pennies of wax and courtesy are gone. Sibrand says: so we go on saying we have one. It has served.

The bishop is called away to a quarrel about a chalice, and the sheet goes under the seal unread. It says everything Sibrand wanted. He carries it down the hill inside his shirt. He does not sing until the boat is past the ferry.

The bishop reads it. He reads the sentence about oaths twice, aloud. The sheet is scraped clean before the ink is dry, and eighty pennies of gifts are not given back. Now the bishop knows what you would have liked to have, Sibrand says. That is a new kind of poor.

You read over his elbow. Twice you put a finger on a word and he changes it without a quarrel: 'among themselves', not 'at their will'. The bishop reads it and finds nothing to scrape. The seal goes on. The chaplain says you have cost him a week of later lawsuits.

The Latin is right; you have seen to that. But the emperor rides tomorrow, and a right sheet without a seal is calfskin. Forty pennies of gifts are gone. Keep the draft, the chaplain says. Kings come back. Sometimes.

You tell Sibrand what the chaplain's friends expect before a seal is so much as warmed. He counts it on his fingers and runs out of fingers. The chest goes home full. It was your tongue, he says. At least it was not our silver.
The bishop's question
The bishop's clerk fetches you from the Stathe. In the hall the bishop has a monk's book open before him and a row of river merchants on the bench, none of them from Tiel.
I stood beside the Tiel men before the emperor. I went down the river with the army for their sake, and came back from Flardinga in a boat, quickly. Nobody may say I am their enemy.
A monk of my diocese writes that at Tiel a false oath is held as nothing. Their church is mine. If souls are being sworn away on my ground I must know it, and not from a book.
You trade there. You are not one of them. So I ask you, before these men: when a stranger claims a debt at Tiel, what happens?
A man from Tiel was at the gate this morning asking who had been called. He left a message for you. It was one word. I think you know the word.
They asked the emperor for a writing this spring and did not get it. I was in the hall. A thing that must be asked for is a thing one did not have.
Brother Alpert says you were plain with him once. I ask you to be as plain with me. It is the same truth; it only stands in a bigger room.
Speak for the bench: they pay the king's toll, bury their dead, and no law forbids a man to drink with his friends
Hand in the Cologne man's claim, and ask only that he be paid
Tell the bishop what you have seen sworn
Say you are a stranger at Tiel and saw nothing worth a bishop's time

You speak for them and you speak well. The king's toll is paid at Tiel to the penny. Their dead are buried from their own chest. The bishop hears you out. That is a defence of their purse, he says, not of their oaths. But it is a defence. He closes the book for today.

You speak for them. The bishop asks whether you have ever seen a debt sworn away there, yes or no. You are slow to answer, and the hall hears how slow. He thanks you coldly. At Tiel they will hear only that you stood up.

You lay Wezelo's sheet before him and ask one thing: nine casks, paid. The bishop reads it and sends a clerk to Tiel that day. The chest pays within the week. Sibrand grumbles for a month, and tells the story as his own idea within a year.

You tell him: the closed fist, the seven hands, the casks. The clerk writes. The bishop says he will send for the priest of Saint Walburg's, and for the men by name. You have just named them. He tells you to come back when the corn is in.

You say you are a small man with a small boat and see little. The bishop looks at you as a man looks at a shut door. Then he calls the next merchant. Outside, the Tiel man at the gate nods once and walks away.
The bishop of Traiectum has asked the merchants of the river how debts are sworn away at Tiel. A monk has written it in a book. The Tiel men say they have the emperor's leave, and drink as before.
The cup goes round
It is a feast day at Tiel and the bench is set out under the toll house wall. A place has been left on it, next to Wigbold. The chest stands open and the big cup is full.
A year, and no brother has cause against you. Two will swear for you; I am one. There is the cloak, there is the cup. After today your oath is seven oaths, anywhere a Tiel keel lies.
Drink it to the bottom. If you leave any, you pay for the cask. If you spill any, you pay for two. Those are the only laws we have that are written down.
You stood up for us in the bishop's hall, where it cost something. The bench heard it by nightfall. I have heard it told four ways since. In all of them you are taller.
You made us pay a stranger what we owed him. I was angry until the Cologne boats came early. A chest needs one key in the hand of a man who can count. Dodo is dead since Lent. Here is his key.
And you told us about the count's ears before you owed us anything. I have not forgotten. I forget very little. It is why they give me the chest.
The new king has made the bishop our count. So the man who asks about our oaths now also holds our court. We shall drink to his health, loudly, and go on as before, quietly.
Take the cup, and the third key of the chest that Sibrand holds out
Take the cup and your share of the year
Count your pound onto the cloak now, and take the cup
Stay a guest of the bench: carry for them, swear for nobody

You drink it to the bottom. Sibrand hangs the key round your neck on a thong and counts out your part: fourteen hundred pennies. The store below London bridge is yours to use as a brother's. Somewhere a monk is writing that the Tiel men judge by their own will. Today their will was you.

You drink it to the bottom. Your pound has come home with company: eight hundred pennies on the cloak. Wigbold swears for you, which makes the bench laugh, and Sibrand after him. From today a debt claimed against you at Tiel meets seven hands.

Your pound goes on the cloak, twelve at a time, and the year's fat is laid beside it: eight hundred and forty in all. Then the cup. From today your oath is seven oaths. Wigbold says you paid late and must tell the first story. You know which one.

You leave the place on the bench empty, and nobody is offended; a guest who knows he is a guest is welcome for ever. Sibrand gives you six casks and the carrying of the bench's wool from London, at double. Wigbold takes you out at low water and shows you where the Waal hides its sand.
The writing is read

The whole bank of Tiel stands before Saint Walburg's door. The priest holds a sheet with the emperor's seal hanging from it and turns the Latin into plain speech, a line at a time. Nobody has brought a cup. That is how you know it is a great day.

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by God's mercy emperor of the Romans. Let all our faithful men know, those now living and those to come. That is how they all begin. Now it is about you.

That the merchants of Tiel may settle among themselves what belongs to their trade. That a stranger's claim against them be heard before the king's man. That they stand in our peace. It is short. Short ones last.

That the merchants of Tiel judge all who trade upon their bank, and that the oath of one, upheld by his fellows, ends a claim. It says so. I have read it three times. God forgive whoever let that sentence through.
My father swore we had it. His father swore it. I have sworn it to a bishop's clerk and felt my ears go red. Now a child can come and look at the seal. It hangs in the church. I had a nail put in.
Send word to that monk at Traiectum. Tell him to come and read it. Tell him the ale-wife will charge him the ordinary price.
Take the seat, and have your house named in the writing among those who asked for it
Take the seat and your share
Take silver for your part, keep the toll freedom, and stay your own man

The priest reads the last line again, slowly: at the asking of Sibrand and of your house, by name. Fifteen hundred pennies from the chest, a seat on the bench, and no toll for your keels at the king's house on the Waal. A sheet of calfskin outlives everyone on this bank. Your name is on it.

You take the place next to Wigbold, and a thousand pennies as your part. The cup comes out after all, once the priest has gone in. From today the Tiel men judge by a writing, and it was your tongue that made them buy it.

Sibrand counts twelve hundred pennies and does not press you. The toll man on the Waal is shown the sheet and told your boat goes under it. You sail before the cask is opened. A man can do a town a great service, Sibrand says, and still not want to live in it.
A page without your name
In the bishop's hall a clerk has a strip of parchment ready and the bishop's ring lies on the table. On the Stathe, a Tiel man you know turns his back as you pass.
The priest of Saint Walburg's has been told what he must ask a Tiel man before he gives him the Body of the Lord. Three have done penance. One paid a Cologne man for nine casks. It is a beginning.
The king has given this church the count's rights over that land. Their court is my court now. They will find that I judge by the law, and that I have read it.
My chapter is finished and has gone to Worms. You are in it, in a way. I wrote 'it is said'. That is you. It is the safest place in a book.
You told the truth where it was dear to tell. Saint Martin does not leave such a man to the mercy of a bench. Say what you want of this church.
Ask the bishop's writing: your keels free of his toll at Traiectum, as Saint Martin's man
Ask ground on the Stathe and a man of the bishop's to keep your store
Ask him to take the false oath from the Tiel men and leave them their cup and their chest

The clerk writes, the ring comes down on the wax. Seven hundred pennies, your keels free at the bishop's toll, and the saint's name over your house. At Tiel they have a name for you too. No man of that bench will swear for you again, or drink where you drink.

Six hundred pennies, a strip of ground on the Stathe with its end in the water, and a bishop's man with a key to keep what you leave there. It is a good plot. The Tiel boats lie two berths down, and their men look through you as through a net.

The bishop is silent, then nearly smiles. The oath is mine, he says. The cup was never my quarrel. He gives you six hundred pennies and his protection. Sibrand hears what you asked. He sends no thanks. But the next Tiel keel you meet dips her yard.
The fort in the marsh
On your way in, at the river mouth, the steward did not come aboard. He waved you into the creek under the round fort, and the count himself came down the mound to look at your boat.
They call it a robber's fort, up the river. I drained this marsh. My men dug every ditch in it. The emperor's army learned the ditches in one afternoon. I have known them all my life.
A toll that an emperor cannot lift is a lawful toll. The Tiel men will say so themselves within ten years. Until then I like to know what they say in the meantime.
His words have been worth more than his cheese money, my lord. We knew of the complaint to the bishop before the bishop did.
I hear somebody at Tiel stood up and said: pay Dirk a sum and be done. I hear the bench did not throw him in the river. That is news. Who was it?
Bring him the bench's offer: a fixed sum each Martinmas, and no Tiel keel searched
Be the count's shipman: his goods in your hold, his men showing you the sands
Ask for silver: a share of this year's toll, counted now

He walks the dyke with you for an hour. Then he names a sum, and it is one the chest can bear. Fifteen hundred pennies to you from both ends of the bargain, his men to show you the Merwede, and at Tiel a place on the bench: the man who ended the toll war drinks free.

He hears it and shakes his head. A sum is fixed; a river grows. He will keep his toll and his searching. But he pays you seven hundred pennies for having tried it, and has his men show you the sands. At Tiel they will know only where you were seen.

Nine hundred pennies, his sign cut on your stem, and two days with his boatmen learning where the Merwede shifts its bed. No toll man from here to the sea will stop you. At Tiel your name is said with another word in front of it, and the word is dog.

The steward counts twelve hundred pennies out of the toll chest, some of them, no doubt, once your own. The boatmen show you the channel because the count tells them to. He does not offer his sign for your stem, and you do not ask.

A river bank in late summer, low evening sun: a Tiel merchant in a good blue cloak holds up a closed fist; six men behind him each raise a hand; an Englishman in a short hooded cape points at wool sacks in a boat; a small Frisian boat alongside.

First light over a river dyke, mist on the water: a long bench under a small stone toll house, full of merchants with wooden cups; an ale-wife with her hand on an open cask; one man standing, arms spread, mid-story; boats drawn up on a timbered bank.

A storehouse door below a timber bridge on the Thames, grey noon: a Frisian in a fur-trimmed cap lays out pairs of gloves on a barrel head beside folded grey and brown cloth and two small kegs; a tally stick in his teeth.

A wide tidal river under a low round fort on a mound, wind and broken cloud: a steward with a rod and a leather purse stands in a small boat's stern, speaking low to the skipper; armed men watch from a jetty; cheeses stacked on the bank.

The Vecht side at Traiectum, a still afternoon: a lean monk of fifty in a black habit sits on a mooring post with a wax tablet on his knee and a stylus raised; the skipper coils a rope and does not look at him; the fort wall behind.

The bank at Tiel, a bright cold day: six men each with a right hand raised; an old merchant gestures to an empty space among them; a Cologne wine seller stands alone by fifteen casks drawn in the mud with a stick; the skipper between.

The strand under Cologne's Roman wall, morning: a broad wine seller in a wine-stained apron stands at a cellar door with arms folded; rows of casks with a burnt mark on each head in the dark behind him; river boats nosed to the gravel.

Inside a timber hall at Tiel, winter firelight: an iron-bound chest with three locks stands open on a table; silver pennies counted in rows on a spread cloak; three men each holding a key; a cask being rolled in at the door, snow outside.

A clerks' room in the palace at Nijmegen, spring light from a narrow window: a chaplain with a ruling stick over a blank sheet of calfskin, quill ready; an old merchant leaning on the table; the skipper at his elbow; a seal press and red wax.

The bishop's hall at Traiectum, a dull day: a bishop of fifty in a plain cope with a book open on a lectern, one finger on the page; a row of uneasy merchants on a wall bench; the skipper standing alone on the floor before him.

The bench under the toll house at Tiel on a feast day, banners of green boughs, clear noon: an old merchant holds out a great two-handled wooden cup to the skipper; an empty place on the bench; the open chest; everyone watching.

Before a small timber church at Tiel, bright morning: a priest holds up a sheet of parchment with a wax seal hanging from it; the whole bank crowded close, caps off; an old merchant with his hand over his mouth; no cup in sight.

The bishop's hall at Traiectum, evening, two candles: a clerk pressing a ring into wax on a strip of parchment; the bishop seated; a monk with a finished book under his arm in the doorway; through the door, a merchant on the quay turning his back.

A creek under a round turf fort in a flat green marsh, wide sky, afternoon: a count of forty in a red cloak, no mail, stands on a dyke looking down into a small boat; straight ditches run to the horizon; a steward with a toll chest.
A great wooden cup, empty, upside down on a bench, with a ring of ale drying on the wood.
An empty place on a crowded bench, and beyond it a small boat loading wool sacks.
A sheet of parchment with an emperor's seal, hung on a nail on a church wall.
An open book on a lectern, a line of small script, and a merchant's shadow across the page.
A boat's stem post with a count's sign newly cut in it, a flat marsh and a round fort behind.
